title: Consumer protection measures questioned
full_text:
The SMSF Association has expressed its concerns over two particular aspects of the government’s proposed superannuation reforms being made with the aim of increasing consumer protection.
The two proposed measures in question are the requirement for SMSFs to hold uniquely identifiable bank accounts and the policy allowing the ATO to provide greater visibility to SMSF trustees, in particular those with low balances, of their returns compared to members of Australian Prudential Regulation Authority-regulated funds.
With reference to the proposal pertaining to bank accounts, SMSF Association chief executive Peter Burgess said the industry body was worried the measure may not consider the approach some trustees use to manage their fund’s financial operations.
“It’s not clear whether they mean a single uniquely identifiable account. We hope that’s not the case because there are plenty of self-managed super funds that have more than one bank account,” Burgess told attendees at the Class Ignite 2026 conference recently held in Sydney.
“So our advice to Treasury would be it shouldn’t be just a single uniquely identifiable account.”
In terms of the ATO having the ability to make available data allowing trustees to compare their fund’s performance with other superannuation sectors, he voiced general support for the proposal, but indicated there was a danger it could have a negative impact.
“We’re not opposing this one. Low balances have been a drag on the performance of the sector [in the past]. We know that people with less than $200,000 in an SMSF have a higher risk of underperforming,” he noted.
“What we are opposed to though is the ATO jumping on these funds in year one because we saw [from] the Class data it’s very common that they may start low, but they build quickly.
“So we don’t want the ATO jumping on them from year one. [However], maybe from year three onwards if they are still low because they’ve been a sub-scale SMSF for an extended period of time, that is not a good outcome. So we’re not opposed to the ATO giving visibility [in that situation].”
author: Darin Tyson-Chan
